strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: predicting human response times under changing time-pressure feedback. Combining learned arithmetic representations with a DRL-modulated evidence accumulator is a plausible and potentially useful application of cognitive structure. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b07/review-experiment-fhwpg3ks/call-e8f05514dfac41958d271988cd167fe5/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The two-day experiment provides substantial repeated behavioral measurements from 36 analyzed participants across four feedback schedules. Examining practice effects and subjective attention/anxiety helps ground the modeling choices in human observations.

Evaluation includes pooled, group-specific, individual-specific, and leave-one-participant-out settings. Figure 3 reports lower average MAPE for the hybrid model in all four settings, including 0.2905 versus 0.3037 under LOPO. The reported training times of 4.42 versus 38.30 minutes on the same hardware also suggest a practical benefit.
weaknesses: Essential methodological details are unavailable in the supplied manuscript. Referenced Appendices S2–S6 are absent, and the main text does not specify the accumulation equations, mapping from SVM predictions to diffusion parameters, RL algorithm, reward function, or training hyperparameters. It also leaves unclear which observations train the no-pressure baseline and whether every fitted stage excludes held-out participants. These omissions prevent reproduction and confident assessment of the central method; promised future code availability does not resolve them.

The comparison does not isolate the contribution of the DDM: Pure DRL removes framewise processing as well as the evidence accumulator. Improvements could therefore arise from temporal representation or action parameterization. Comparisons with a matched sequential neural model, a stimulus-conditioned conventional DDM, and supervised response-time regressors are needed. The related-work rationale also understates existing DDMs' predictive capabilities and recurrent networks' ability to process changing inputs, leaving the specific advance insufficiently established.

The evidence supports response-time prediction more directly than the claimed frame-level cognitive explanation. Many different accumulation trajectories can produce the same terminal response time, and no independent evidence identifies the learned trajectories as human cognitive dynamics. Figure 3 even shows nonzero 'time pressure effect' trajectories in the no-pressure group, suggesting that the agent may also correct baseline prediction errors. Agreement with aggregate group trends does not validate the proposed habituation explanation. Stimulus ablations and predictions under different within-trial timing schedules would help test this central claim.

The predictive improvements over Pure DRL are modest: pooled MAPE decreases from 0.3034 to 0.2999, while LOPO decreases from 0.3037 to 0.2905. No confidence intervals or adequately described repeated-run analysis establish their reliability across participants and training runs. The efficiency comparison likewise lacks uncertainty and a common predictive-performance stopping criterion. LOPO is valuable, but shuffled trial splits and selected chronological examples do not establish prospective temporal generalization.

The behavioral conclusions require more restraint. Groups contain only 7–10 analyzed participants, and the criteria for excluding three extreme outliers are unspecified. The reported significant random-versus-none comparison does not establish that random feedback is superior to every other schedule, while nonsignificant accuracy differences do not establish equivalence. Exclusion-sensitivity analyses and participant-level uncertainty would strengthen these conclusions. As a smaller reporting correction, the abstract should distinguish 50 recruited participants from the 36 actually analyzed.
